ai-at-work.title: Cybersecurity AI startup Corma reaches $1B valuation in about 3 months
ai-at-work.excerpt: Three months since introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corba has raised a $125 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Corma hit unicorn status in roughly 90 days by raising $125 million for its AI-powered cybersecurity platform. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because it signals where venture capital thinks the real pain points are, and spoiler alert, it's securing your increasingly messy hybrid infrastructure. I'll believe the valuation is justified when they've actually stopped a breach, not just impressed investors with PowerPoint slides about what AI *could* do.

ai-at-work.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security
ai-at-work.excerpt: Trump contradicted his own government's intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Jensen Huang's wife apparently had intelligence connections to China, Trump said it wasn't a security threat, and his own intel officials disagreed with him. This matters to digital workplace folks because it's a stark reminder that C-suite backgrounds and security clearances affect everyone downstream, especially in tech companies handling sensitive data and infrastructure. Look, I've been around long enough to know that when leadership and government agencies can't agree on basic security facts, somebody's workplace policies are about to get a lot more complicated.

ai-at-work.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in ‘under three hours’
ai-at-work.excerpt: The FBI says that the open source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Someone built an open source hacking tool called Artex AI that apparently works so fast it can breach enterprise networks in less than three hours, and the FBI is now warning that it's already being used in real attacks against major targets. This matters because your workplace infrastructure, no matter how fancy your digital workplace platform is, sits on top of networks that can be compromised faster than most organizations can respond to alerts. The irony here is thick: we spend millions on employee experience platforms while someone's free GitHub project can unlock the whole thing before lunch.

ai-at-work.title: With $5M in funding, Pretxt launches runtime oversight layer to supervise AI agents in real time
ai-at-work.excerpt: Artificial intelligence supervision pioneer Pretxt AI is launching with $5 million in seed funding today as it tries to contain the very real risk of unleashing autonomous agents in production environ
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Pretxt AI just launched with five million dollars to build oversight tools that watch AI agents while they're actually running in production, making sure they don't go rogue and break your company's rules. This matters because we're all about to deploy autonomous AI agents into our workflows, and nobody wants to explain to the board why an unsupervised bot decided to send confidential emails to competitors. I'll believe the guardrails work when I see them, but honestly, adding supervision layers to AI is probably cheaper than the lawsuit that follows when you don't.

tools-tech.title: 6 Chrome settings tweaks every power user needs to know
tools-tech.excerpt: For improved privacy and security, fewer interruptions, and enhanced productivity, I highly recommend changing these default browser settings.
tools-tech.dwp_take: ZDNet ran a piece highlighting six Chrome settings adjustments that supposedly unlock better privacy, security, and productivity for power users. This matters because your browser is basically your digital workplace now, and most people never touch settings beyond the defaults, leaving themselves exposed and distracted. Here's the thing though: if you need an article to tell you to adjust your browser settings, you're probably not the power user the headline thinks you are, but you should read it anyway because the advice is sound and takes five minutes.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft blames major outage on a July update defect – and two other factors
tools-tech.excerpt: A surprise defect took more than 80% of Microsoft’s servers out at the outage’s peak. Here’s what happened.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft's July update contained a defect that knocked out over 80% of their servers at peak impact, compounded by two additional factors in their infrastructure. This matters because when Microsoft goes down, so does a huge chunk of the world's digital workplace infrastructure, leaving IT teams scrambling to manage angry users who can't access Teams, Outlook, or anything else running on Azure. After three decades watching companies blame "perfect storm" scenarios, I'll say this: having a defect slip through that takes out four-fifths of your servers suggests someone skipped a few steps in their testing process.

tools-tech.title: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’
tools-tech.excerpt: Underground brokers are selling access to hijacked enterprise AI accounts, with companies footing the usage bill, Google reports.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Underground criminals are selling stolen access to enterprise AI accounts, leaving companies to pay the bills while bad actors run up charges on their dime. This matters because most digital workplace teams haven't locked down AI tool access the way they should, and attackers know it. Here's the brutal truth: you've probably got employees sharing credentials, using the same password everywhere, and nobody's tracking who actually has access to what. That's not a security problem. That's an invitation.

tools-tech.title: Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
tools-tech.excerpt: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services, including Outlook, E
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft's outage gave cybercriminals the perfect cover story to convince people their login credentials were compromised and needed resetting, resulting in a coordinated phishing campaign that hit multiple industries right after the legitimate service went down. This matters because every real outage becomes a window of vulnerability where your employees are already stressed and primed to believe something went wrong, making them far more likely to click malicious links or enter credentials into fake portals. After thirty years in this space, I can tell you that the worst part isn't Microsoft's downtime, it's that your security training probably didn't prepare people to stay skeptical during actual emergencies, which is exactly when attackers know you'll be sloppy.

digital-culture.title: The probable future is bleak. It’s time for improbable futures
digital-culture.excerpt: Massed protesters, enraged by hunger and joblessness, loot shops along the Boulevard Saint-Germain. A crowd marches on the Interior Ministry and is driven back with bayonets. Students tear their schoo
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is warning that if we don't change course, we're heading toward social unrest driven by economic inequality and joblessness. For digital workplace pros, this means your organization's resilience and how you treat remote workers actually matters beyond the quarterly earnings call. Here's the thing: building an inclusive digital workplace isn't woke posturing, it's basic business continuity planning for a world that's getting angrier by the day.

digital-culture.title: The ‘recession indicators’ visible at your workplace
digital-culture.excerpt: People all over the U.S. have been sharing their “personal recession indicators” in recent months, from only being able to afford Goldfish crackers and water for lunch to filling up their cars with a
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company reported on workplace-level recession signals that go beyond traditional economic data, like reduced hiring, frozen budgets, and changes in employee spending habits. Digital workplace leaders need to pay attention to these signals because they directly impact everything from tool adoption rates to collaboration patterns and remote work policies that suddenly get scrutinized. Here's the thing: if your CFO is suddenly asking why you need three communication platforms when one will do, that's not a question about efficiency, that's your recession indicator flashing red on the dashboard.

digital-culture.title: Stressful jobs do, in fact, pay more. But there’s a catch
digital-culture.excerpt: Do more stressful jobs come with a bigger paycheck? It depends. According to a recent study conducted by online resume building platform Resume Genius, the most stressful jobs pay an average of 62% mo
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new study shows stressful jobs pay 62% more on average than low-stress ones, though the benefit varies wildly by education level. This matters to digital workplace folks because we're the ones designing tools and policies meant to make high-stress environments more bearable, so understanding the stress-pay trade-off shapes how we position wellness features and flexibility options. Here's the thing: paying people more to be miserable is just old-school thinking with a bigger number attached, and smart companies are figuring out that remote work and async collaboration might actually be the better raise.

digital-culture.title: Four ways work was better in the ’90s
digital-culture.excerpt: The fundamentals of work remain remarkably stable over time. For both our hunter-gatherer ancestors and modern chief AI ethicists, work was, and still is, a critical way to translate skill, effort, an
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company argues that certain aspects of work culture were genuinely better in the 1990s, pointing to how fundamentals like skill-to-reward translation and status through competence remain constant even as the cultural context shifts. This matters because digital workplace leaders need to understand what actually made the 90s workplace function better so we can deliberately recreate those elements instead of just nostalgia-posting on LinkedIn. Personally, I think the article's onto something: people got paid closer to what they were worth, meetings had agendas, and nobody expected you to Slack at 11 PM, which isn't retro thinking, it's just common sense.

industry-news.title: Italy Fines Meta $887M Over Facebook Android Photo Access
industry-news.excerpt: Italy fines Meta $887M over Facebook's Android photo access. Learn what the consent ruling means for European users and app developers. The post Italy Fines Meta $887M Over Facebook Android Photo Acce
industry-news.dwp_take: Italy's antitrust authority hit Meta with an $887 million fine because Facebook was accessing photos on Android devices without properly getting user consent first. This matters to digital workplace folks because it signals that European regulators are actually enforcing data privacy rules with real teeth, which means your organization needs to audit how your apps and tools handle user permissions or face similar consequences. Meta getting fined nearly a billion dollars for something that sounds almost quaint by today's privacy standards is both hilarious and terrifying, depending on whether your company's legal team has been sleeping on consent protocols.

industry-news.title: OPPO’s Next Big Bet: Three Devices That Break the Smartphone Mold
industry-news.excerpt: OPPO is reportedly developing a 16:9 smartphone, wider Find N7 foldable and pocket gimbal camera. Here's what the rumors reveal about its upcoming devices. The post OPPO’s Next Big Bet: Three Devices
industry-news.dwp_take: OPPO is working on three experimental devices: a 16:9 aspect ratio phone, an expanded foldable, and a pocket gimbal camera, according to TechRepublic's reporting on the rumors. For digital workplace folks, this matters because it shows how consumer device makers are actively reshaping the form factors we'll eventually support on our networks and in our mobile device management strategies. Honestly, I've seen enough "smartphone mold breaking" announcements over three decades to know that most of these experiments become expensive paperweights while one or two actually change how people work, so I'll believe it when I see adoption numbers.

industry-news.title: Apple HomeView Is Here: Is the $299 Smart Display Worth It?
industry-news.excerpt: Apple HomeView is here for $299. We review early impressions, Siri AI performance, smart-home features, and privacy concerns to decide whether it's worth buying. The post Apple HomeView Is Here: Is th
industry-news.dwp_take: Apple just dropped HomeView, a $299 smart display that promises to handle your smart home setup while Siri watches over everything. For those of us managing digital workspaces, this matters because smart displays are increasingly becoming command centers for hybrid work, controlling everything from lighting to meeting room availability. Here's the thing though: paying $299 for Apple's privacy promises feels a bit like paying extra for a car that claims not to track where you drive, then reading the fine print.

industry-news.title: WHOOP Launches Free Social Network for Sharing Health and Fitness Data
industry-news.excerpt: Whoop launches Humans, a social network that lets members share fitness and health data with friends. Here's how it works and what to know about privacy. The post WHOOP Launches Free Social Network fo
industry-news.dwp_take: WHOOP just launched Humans, a social network where people can share their fitness and health data with friends, effectively turning personal biometrics into social currency. This matters to digital workplace folks because employee wellness programs are increasingly intertwined with company culture and engagement platforms, which means you're about to field requests from HR about integrating this into your digital ecosystem. Here's my take: before you get excited about another social network, ask yourself if your employees actually want their resting heart rate broadcast to coworkers, because I've got news for you, they probably don't.
